name: Triamcinolone injections

lead: Triamcinolone is a corticosteroid that dermatologists inject into patches of alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of hair loss, to regrow hair in the patch. It is not used for ordinary pattern hair loss.

It is about five times as potent as cortisol and calms the local immune attack on follicles. A 2020 systematic review reported more than half regrowth in about 81 percent of treated patients, though hair often regrows on its own in patchy disease.

paras: It is given in a dermatologist's office as repeated injections into the bald patches, with regrowth judged over the following weeks to months.
It is prescription-only. Skin thinning is commonly described with skin injections, and injection near the eye has caused raised eye pressure and cases of endophthalmitis.

angle.text: Dermatologists inject triamcinolone into patches of alopecia areata to calm the immune attack on follicles so hair regrows in the patch. A 2020 review reported more than half regrowth in about 81 percent of treated patients.

lead: Triamcinolone acetonide is a synthetic glucocorticoid, about five times as potent as cortisol, sold under brand names such as Kenalog [1]. Dermatologists inject it into the skin (intralesional) to settle inflammation in a specific spot, and people seek it out for several appearance concerns: bald patches from alopecia areata, thick keloid and hypertrophic scars, and individual inflamed acne nodules [1][2][3].

For hair, the injection is placed into patches of alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, and sometimes into thinning eyebrows. The aim is to calm the local immune attack so that hair can regrow in the patch [2]. A 2020 systematic review cited by Wikipedia found that about 81 percent of patients receiving triamcinolone injections achieved more than half regrowth, while the same article notes that hair often regrows spontaneously in patchy disease, which complicates judging treatment effects [2].

Beyond hair, triamcinolone is one of the most common injections in cosmetic dermatology: it is used to flatten raised scars, to shrink painful acne cysts, and as part of treatment of other scalp and facial inflammatory conditions [1][3][4][5]. Its use for keloids was reported in the mid-1960s, and it remains a standard option alongside surgery, pressure, silicone, cryotherapy and radiation [1][6]. It is a prescription medicine administered by clinicians in the US, UK and EU [1]. Forum members also mention it in connection with injuries, where cortisone shots are a topic of debate among lifters [7][8].
infobox: Intralesional injection (also joint, intravitreal, topical, nasal)
Alopecia areata patches, keloids and hypertrophic scars, inflamed acne nodules
Prescription-only in US, UK, EU; OTC nasal spray in US since 2014 [1]

paras: For appearance, a main use is intralesional injection into patches of alopecia areata, and sometimes eyebrow loss, though Wikipedia says efficacy in small scalp patches or eyebrow lesions is uncertain [2]. Injections are typically small and numerous across the patch and are repeated at intervals by the treating clinician. Alopecia areata affects about 0.15 percent of people at any time and about 2 percent at some point in life, usually beginning in childhood, and Wikipedia describes its main burden as psychological, including loss of self-image [2]. Forum posts also mention steroid injections for scalp bumps and for frontal fibrosing alopecia along the hairline, in which a hair-loss condition is treated with injections along the frontal hairline [9][10].

Intralesional triamcinolone is a long-standing treatment for hypertrophic scars and keloids, where it is used to soften and flatten raised tissue [1][3]. Wikipedia describes the injection as reducing fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching, and says it was introduced in the mid-1960s [6]. Hypertrophic scars stay within the original wound boundary and usually fade over one to two years, while keloids grow beyond it; corticosteroid injection is listed as one option for hypertrophic scars that keep thickening [11]. Keloids occur in an estimated 15 to 20 percent of people of sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latino ancestry and much less often in people of European background, and about a third of patients have an affected first-degree relative [6]. Surgical excision alone is associated with recurrence rates of 70 to 100 percent, which is why excision is often combined with other therapies; Wikipedia also says corticosteroids are not recommended for children because of growth risks [6].

Trials compare it with other injectables: a 2014 comparison of intralesional verapamil and triamcinolone in hypertrophic scars and keloids [3], and a 2023 single-blinded randomized trial of triamcinolone alone versus a verapamil-triamcinolone mixture in keloids arising from surgical incisions, treated until nearly flat or for up to eight sessions [4]. A 2018 randomized comparison tested extracorporeal shockwave therapy for keloid scars as an alternative approach [12].

Dermatologists commonly inject dilute triamcinolone into large inflamed acne nodules to reduce their size and pain more quickly than they would settle alone. A survey of 100 dermatology professionals reported on the concentrations and volumes clinicians use and noted little published data or consensus on best practice [5]. A trial examined cold anesthesia to reduce pain during intralesional steroid injection for nodulocystic acne [13]. Reviews also describe triamcinolone injections for hidradenitis suppurativa lesions [14], seborrheic dermatitis [15], and eyelid retraction in thyroid eye disease [16].
Other routes include intra-articular, intravitreal and nasal products, plus topical creams and dental pastes. These are medical uses not related to appearance [1].

In alopecia areata, the 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis (Yee et al.) summarized by Wikipedia reported more than 50 percent regrowth in about 81 percent of treated patients [2]. Wikipedia cautions that spontaneous regrowth is common in patchy disease: in more than half of sudden-onset patchy cases hair regrows within a year, and with one or two patches up to 80 percent recover within a year [2]. For hidradenitis suppurativa, a 2025 systematic review of six studies (313 patients, 527 lesions) of ultrasound-guided injections reported a pooled clinical response rate of 80.5 percent, with 69.8 percent of lesions completely healed [14]. For keloids, the 2023 randomized trial compared triamcinolone alone with a triamcinolone-verapamil blend [4].

Dermatologists surveyed about acne injections reported that hypopigmentation and skin atrophy (thinning, indentation) are the effects most often discussed with patients; about half counsel patients on these before every injection, and 88.8 percent said fewer than one percent of patients returned with a problem [5].

Systemic effects can include menstrual irregularities because the drug binds the progesterone receptor [1]. Corticosteroids as a class are associated with Cushing-type changes, raised blood sugar, bone loss, infection risk and mood effects with prolonged systemic exposure, and are contraindicated in pregnancy [17]. Other sites carry different risks: intravitreal use has raised eye pressure and been linked to noninfectious endophthalmitis in a case series of seven patients [1][18], and a meta-analysis of suprachoroidal triamcinolone examined eye-pressure effects [19]. Case reports describe crystalline maculopathy after eye injections [20].

Corticosteroids entered medicine with cortisone in 1948, followed by hydrocortisone (1951), prednisone and prednisolone (1955) and dexamethasone and betamethasone (1958); Reichstein, Kendall and Hench shared the 1950 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on adrenal hormones [17]. Triamcinolone acetonide is a more potent halogenated derivative developed in this later wave of synthetic steroids [1]. Its use in keloids was reported by Griffith in 1966 [1], and the US nasal-spray form (Nasacort) became available over the counter in 2014 [1].

Triamcinolone acetonide is a glucocorticoid receptor agonist with little mineralocorticoid activity. Wikipedia lists its potency at about five times cortisol and about eight times prednisone, with affinity for androgen and estrogen receptors under 0.1 percent of testosterone and estradiol and about 15 percent of progesterone's at the progesterone receptor [1]. It is metabolized in the liver and excreted mainly in urine (about 75 percent) and feces (about 25 percent) [1]. Chemically it is a halogenated cyclic ketal pregnane corticosteroid [1].

A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis (Yee et al.) summarized by Wikipedia reported more than 50 percent regrowth in about 81 percent of patients on intralesional injections [2]. Registered trials include a 2007 phase 2 study of adrenal function with intralesional triamcinolone in 18 patients with alopecia areata (NCT00484679) and a 2009 phase 2 study of combined Restylane and triamcinolone injections in 14 patients with alopecia areata (NCT01797432); results are not summarized here [21][22].

A 2014 trial compared intralesional verapamil and triamcinolone in hypertrophic scars and keloids [3], a 2023 randomized trial compared triamcinolone alone and combined with verapamil in keloids [4], and a registered phase 4 trial (NCT01720056, 14 participants, terminated) compared verapamil and steroid to prevent keloid recurrence [23]. A 2025 systematic review of a related technique covers trapdoor deformity after facial skin flap reconstruction, where triamcinolone is among the treatments [24].

The 2023 keloid trial and 2014 verapamil comparison form part of a broader literature on combining triamcinolone with other agents; Wikipedia notes that combined triple therapy with 5-fluorouracil and pulsed dye laser has been reported to improve results in adults [4][3][6]. For alopecia areata beyond injections, Wikipedia lists topical minoxidil and, since 2022, JAK inhibitors approved by the FDA (baricitinib in June 2022, ritlecitinib in June 2023, deuruxolitinib in July 2024) [2].

Triamcinolone acetonide is available as a generic and is prescription-only in the EU and UK, available by prescription or over the counter depending on product in the US and Canada, and Schedule 4 in Australia [1]. Brand names include Kenalog, Nasacort and Xipere [1]. Kenalog also appears in bodybuilding and lifting forums, where posters describe it in connection with sports injuries, scar tissue pain and cortisone shots, with some advising against corticosteroids during tendon rehab [7][8][25][26]. A review in Wikipedia's corticosteroid entry cites a meta-analysis finding small, transient pain relief from corticosteroid injection in rotator cuff tendinosis [17]. In veterinary medicine it is used for itching in dogs, and it has featured in horse-racing drug-test cases, including a 2019 case involving the Champion Hurdle favourite Yanworth [1].

On T Nation and similar forums, triamcinolone is mentioned mostly second-hand: as the shot a doctor gave for a scar, a bump on the scalp or a sports injury. Alopecia-areata and beard-patch threads treat it as something dermatologists do rather than something self-managed [9][27].

lore.intro: Steroid injections come up in discussions of alopecia areata, eyebrow and beard-patch thinning, scars and injuries on forums such as T Nation, usually as something a doctor does.

claims.claim: Triamcinolone injections regrow patchy hair loss
A shot can flatten a keloid or stubborn scar
A cortisone shot can speed up a pimple or bump
Corticosteroid injections are unwelcome for athletes recovering from injury
Keloids come back after being cut out, so injection is used to keep them down
JAK inhibitors have replaced injections for alopecia areata

timeline.event: Cortisone introduced into medicine, beginning the corticosteroid era.[17]
Reichstein, Kendall and Hench share the Nobel Prize for adrenal hormone work.[17]
Intralesional triamcinolone for keloid reported by Griffith.[1]
Phase 2 registration of adrenal function with intralesional triamcinolone in alopecia areata (NCT00484679).[21]
Comparison of intralesional verapamil and triamcinolone in hypertrophic scars and keloids; US OTC nasal spray approved.[1][3]
Systematic review of intralesional triamcinolone in alopecia areata reports regrowth in most treated patients.[2]
Survey of 100 dermatology professionals on intralesional triamcinolone for acne published.[5]
FDA authorizes the first JAK inhibitor for severe alopecia areata (baricitinib).[2]
